content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes the prompt-tuning method for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), where, during model-tuning with down-stream datasets, the pre-trained parameters of GNNs keep unchanged while few parameters for prompt-tuning are trained along with classification layers. To realize this graph prompt-tuning mechanism, the authors first define the prompt-tuning scheme for graph-structured data, and then introduce the specific prompt-tuning technique: adding learnable parameters to node features. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed GPF by showing that it approximates any graph transformation, but also showing that it makes comparable performances to the expensive fine-tuning scheme over various pre-trained GNNs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
* The proposed graph prompt-tuning mechanism is general, well-defined, and novel. 
* The authors provide the theoretical analysis that the proposed GPF can approximate any graph transformation, which is convincing. 
* The proposed GPF shows comparable performances against expensive fine-tuning, and sometimes outperforms them. 
* This paper is well-written, and easy to follow. 

### Weaknesses, which are mostly suggestions to further improve the paper.
* I suggest authors to add an analysis on which properties the trained graph-prompt-features learn. I know it is difficult to analyze, however, it is unclear why the graph-prompt-features are helpful for down-stream tasks. Thus, analyzing such the property would be beneficial. 
* It is unclear and not convincing why the authors do not experimentally compare the previous graph prompt-tuning work, namely GPPT (Sun et al., 2022). I know the prompt-tuning mechanism of the proposed GPF is more general and different from the previous GPPT, however, I suggest authors to make the experimental comparisons.
* I suggest authors to add extra analyses on varying the number of tuning datasets. One of the advantages of the prompt-tuning scheme is that the prompted model can have high generalization performances on specific datasets with only few tuning samples, however, the evaluated experimental settings have the large number of tuning samples (i.e., all training samples). Thus, it would be beneficial to analyze whether the proposed GPF can have strong generalization performance with few tuning samples, as in language domains with language models [1]. 
* I suggest authors to add explanations on the extra linear layer for classification in the main paper. In particular, compared to the prompt-tuning for generative language models (e.g., GPT-3), the proposed graph prompt-tuning scheme requires extra classification layers, which should be trained along with prompt features. I think such points should be further highlighted (i.e., I found explanations on classification layers in Appendix, but I suggest authors to move that part to the main paper as well).

---

[1] The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning, EMNLP 2021.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer wghj,

we really appreciate your comments and your support for our work. We hope our response can address your concerns. Please find our detailed response below.

**Suggestion 1.** Adding an analysis on which properties the trained graph-prompt-features learn.

Your suggestion is rather considerable but requires extensive further research. We think the key point is to find a metric to determine how effective a pre-trained GNN model will perform on a specific downstream task, but we have not found such a suitable metric yet.

**Suggestion 2.** Comparison with GPPT [1].

We have conducted some experiments with GPPT but did not get meaningful results. GPPT requires that the pre-trained models apply link prediction as their pre-training task, but only a small number of existing pre-trained GNN models satisfy this requirement. Besides, most pre-trained GNN models focus on the graph classification task, while GPPT is designed for node classification. To align GPPT with the graph classification task, we try some simple readout functions (sum, mean, max, LSTM) to obtain graph representations, but all of them get poor performance. This is why we do not show the results of GPPT in our paper.

**Suggestion 3.** Adding few-shot learning tasks.

Thanks for your suggestion. Adding few-shot learning tasks that only contain a few training examples is our future direction. We are still designing proper graph few-shot learning tasks for pre-trained GNN models now.

**Suggestion 4.** Adding further explanations on the extra linear layer for classification in the main paper.

Thanks for your detailed suggestion. We will move some explanations from the Appendix to the main paper.

**Minor point 1.** It is worthwhile to add supporting evidence when describing the fundamental challenges of GNNs in the first paragraph of the Introduction by mentioning existing works.

Thanks for your suggestion. We have added more related papers in our latest revision.

**Minor point 2.** The reference to Figure 1 is missing.

Thanks for your careful check. We have added the reference to Figure 1 in our latest revision.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer mcky,

we hope our point-to-point response can address your concerns and clarify our contribution.

**Weakness 1.** Prompt turning is not necessary.

Designing deeper and larger graph neural networks is an inevitable trend for training effective GNN models [1, 2]. As the scale of the model increases, the parameters involved in fine-tuning also increase, but the parameter cost of our proposed GPF is almost unchanged, which shows a promising prospect. Furthermore, graph prompt tuning is not only parameter-efficient but also can achieve performance improvement in some cases, according to the experimental results in our paper. We hope that our research on graph prompt tuning can provide a new alternative for the adaptation of the pre-trained GNN models and inspire researchers to think about how to use the pre-train models better.

**Weakness 2.** One of the motivation is not true.

Pre-trained GNN models tend to stack more layers than normal ones [3], e.g., GNN models directly trained on Cora, CiteSeer, PubMed, ogbn, and PPI usually contain no more than 3 layers. In comparison, pre-trained GNN models usually contain at least 5 layers. Pre-trained GNN models (mostly no less than 256) also tend to have larger hidden size compared to normal models (mostly no more than 64). This is why we say pre-trained GNN models usually contain several times the parameters of the normal models.

**Weakness 3.** Graph pre-training does not contain as much useful information as it in NLP.

Honestly speaking, explaining the nature of graph pre-training needs further research. We think your concern lies in the effectiveness of pre-trained GNN models, which is beyond the scope of our paper. Given that pre-trained GNN models achieve satisfactory results on many tasks, we assume that pre-training GNN models is meaningful and effective. Our paper aims to transfer the idea of prompt tuning to the pre-trained GNN models and proposes an alternative tuning method during the adaptation stage. Similar to the advanced works [4, 5] in the image field, we freeze the parameters of the pre-trained model, while transforming the input of the downstream task. The experimental results indicate that our graph prompt tuning method can be regarded as a considerable tuning method and has a promising prospect.

**Weakness 4.** The main results are far from those in GROVER [6].

The experiment setting used in our paper is different from that in GROVER [6], which leads to a huge result gap. Specifically, GROVER applies 11 million unlabelled molecules to pre-train the model, while we follow the pre-training strategy proposed in Hu et al [7]. and use 2 million unlabelled molecules to pre-train the model. Our setting is more widely used in existing work [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12], and it makes us easier to compare and draw general conclusions.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer q8DN,

we appreciate your comments. We hope our response can address your concerns. Please find our detailed response below.

**Concern 1.** It seems using the term of prompt is inappropriate.

We agree with your opinion that prompt tuning can adapt the pre-trained model to different kinds of downstream tasks. As for your suggestion to apply GPF on more tasks, it is limited by the fact that most existing pre-trained GNN models are trained and used on protein graphs or molecular graphs for graph property prediction (a kind of graph classification). Similar to the advanced works [1, 2] in the image field, our paper aims to explore whether the prompt tuning (freezing the pre-trained models while transforming the input) can work on the adaptation of pre-trained GNN models.

As your suggestion to compare the performance of GPF with fine-tuning the same number of parameters of the pre-trained model, it is nearly impossible to achieve in practice because the number of parameters used in GPF is much smaller than that of any single linear transformation in the pre-trained model, which means the number of parameters of any part of the pre-trained model far exceeds the number of parameters used in GPF. Therefore, we can not conduct such a comparison.

**Concern 2.** The results in Table 2 should be further discussed.

All these pre-training strategies in Table 2 are proposed by Hu et al [3]. Practically, people select an optimal one from all these candidates according to the performance on the downstream task. This is why we compare the optimal results of fine-tuning with the optimal results of GPF in our paper. Under such comparison, GPF outperforms fine-tuning in 2/8 of the downstream tasks and has a drop of no more than 2\% on average in the remains. Therefore, we claim the results are comparable. We guess your concern lies in the pair-wise comparison of GPF and fine-tuning. As for the pair-wise comparison of GPF and fine-tuning, it seems GPF can not outperform fine-tuning in most cases and have a significant drop in some cases, which is inevitable due to the uncertainty in the performance of pre-trained models on downstream tasks. Specifically, these pre-training strategies do not always have a positive effect on downstream tasks, which can be demonstrated by the fact that some pre-trained models can not outperform the blank models with random initialization. If the pre-training strategy has little effect on the downstream task, GPF can only tune a small number of parameters and may not achieve satisfactory performance. This is why some GPF results show a significant drop compared to fine-tuning.

**Concern 3**. Why link transformation and isolated component transformations are two separate steps? 

The critical difference between link transformation and isolated component transformation is that link transformation adds or removes edges between existing nodes, while isolated component transformation adds new nodes to the initial graph or removes existing nodes from the initial graph. Link transformation cannot include the graph-level transformation that adds or removes nodes to the initial graph.

**Minor point 1.** The reference format of InfoGraph Sun et al. (2019) in Section 2.1 is not consistent. 

Thanks for your detailed suggestion. We have fixed it in our latest revision.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper claims to do prompt tuning for graph neural networks (GNNs), on graph classification tasks.
It trains a task-specific feature which is called GP-feature (GPF) to add perturbations to the feature space of the downstream graphs. 
It theoretically proves that GPF can achieve the approximately equivalent effect of graph-level transformation (including feature/link/isolated component transformations). 
In experiments, the paper mainly compare GPF with fine-tuning, and the results are not good.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
+ The idea is simple to follow. 
+ Theoretical analysis is provided. 
+ The reduction of parameter size is huge, in comparison to fine-tuning. 

Weakness
- The motivation is not clear. Why the approach considered in this paper is called graph tuning? It fails to establish the connection w.r.t. prompt used in NLP. In NLP, prompts are used to reformulate the downstream tasks as a masked language modeling problem. The consistency between prompt tuning problem and the original pretraining masked language modeling problem then allows better performance to be obtained. However, in this paper, the authors consider graph classification, and the use of graph prompt does not change the form of graph classification. GPF is more like a new transformation trick to be added to the feature space, which has nothing to with prompt. 

- The experimental results are not enough. It only compares with fine-tuning, and the results are usually not comparable. The current results are hard to persuade readers that GPF performs well. Besides, why not compare with the closely related GPPT (KDD 2022)? 

- The implementation details are unclear. What are the exact hyperparameter settings? How to train the GPF?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The authors provide codes, but more implementation details should be added into the appendix. 

One unclear part:
On page 4, "we obtain a pre-trained GNN encoder f(G)", what is G? It is in bold, which is not introduced before.

content.comment:
Dear Reviewer Vc2p,

we hope our point-to-point response can address your concerns and clarify our contribution.

**Weakness 1.** The motivation is not clear. 

We agree with your opinion that the original purpose of prompt tuning is to narrow the gap between the pre-training tasks and the downstream tasks [1]. However, with the development of prompt methods, this motivation has further extension. For example, people find that prompt tuning is also effective for BERT with a low coefficient weight of the masked language model [2]. Meanwhile, Prefix-Tuning [3] applies layer-wise learnable prompts in each middle layer. It is hard to say the gap between the pre-training and downstream tasks has been narrowed in these cases. Thus, prompt tuning can also be regarded as a new kind of tuning method which freezes the pre-trained model but tunes the input during the adaptation on downstream tasks. The key point of this thought is that the pre-trained model is general and capable, which should be retained as much as possible during the adaptation stage. This thought inspires some transferring applications of prompt tuning in other areas. In the image field, some advanced works [4, 5] change the input image rather than fine-tune the pre-trained models and achieve satisfactory results. Their prompt methods also show no connection with the pre-training task. Our paper transfers the idea of input transformation to the pre-trained GNN models so that we can call the method in our paper a prompt method for GNNs.

**Weakness 2.** The experimental results are not enough.

The results in Table 3 and Table 4 indicate the consistent superiority of GPF compared to fine-tuning.
We guess your concern mainly lies in the results in Table 2. All these pre-training strategies in Table 2 are proposed by Hu et al [6]. Practically, people select an optimal one from all these candidates according to the performance on the downstream task. This is why we compare the optimal results of fine-tuning with the optimal results of GPF in our paper. Under such comparison, GPF outperforms fine-tuning in 2/8 of the downstream tasks and has a drop of no more than 2% on average in the remains. Therefore, we claim the results are comparable. As for the pair-wise comparison of GPF and fine-tuning, it seems GPF can not outperform fine-tuning in most cases and may have a significant drop, which is inevitable due to the uncertainty in the performance of pre-trained models on downstream tasks. Specifically, these pre-training strategies do not always have a positive effect on downstream tasks, which can be demonstrated by the fact that some pre-trained models can not outperform the blank models with random initialization. If the pre-training strategy has little effect on the downstream task, GPF can only tune a small number of parameters and may not achieve satisfactory performance. This is why some GPF results show a significant drop compared to fine-tuning.

As for the comparison with GPPT [7], we conducted some experiments but have yet to get meaningful results. GPPT requires that the pre-trained models apply link prediction as their pre-training task, but only a small number of existing pre-trained GNN models satisfy this requirement. Besides, most pre-trained GNN models focus on the graph classification task, while GPPT is designed for node classification. To align GPPT with the graph classification task, we try some simple readout functions (sum, mean, max, LSTM) to obtain graph representations, but all of them get poor performance. This is why we do not show the results of GPPT in our paper.
